nameStory: The 'spotted' part is easy to see - look for the silvery-white markings that splash across each heart-shaped leaf like paint splatters! It's called a 'deadnettle' because while it looks similar to stinging nettle, it won't sting you at all - the leaves are completely harmless to touch.
description: Spotted deadnettle is a low-growing perennial herb that spreads along the ground, forming colorful carpets in shaded areas. The plant grows about 6-12 inches tall with distinctive heart-shaped leaves marked by silvery-white spots or stripes down their centers. From spring through fall, it produces clusters of small, tubular flowers that are typically pink, purple, or white, arranged in whorls around the square stems.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with distinctive silvery-white markings down the center, arranged in opposite pairs. The leaves feel soft and velvety, with toothed edges and a slightly wrinkled texture.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, two-lipped tubular flowers clustered in whorls around the stem, typically pink, purple, or white. The upper lip forms a hood while the lower lip is spotted and serves as a landing platform for bees.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that creep along the ground via runners. Stems root at nodes where they touch soil, creating new plants and dense colonies.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that are characteristic of the mint family - you can feel the four distinct edges when you roll the stem between your fingers. Stems are often reddish-purple in color.

habitat: Spotted deadnettle thrives in partial to full shade in moist, rich soils. You'll commonly find it in woodland edges, under shrubs, along shaded paths, and in cultivated gardens where it often escapes from landscaping. It prefers areas with consistent moisture and protection from harsh afternoon sun.

seasonality.spring: Fresh new growth emerges with bright silvery leaf markings most pronounced. First flowers appear in late spring, typically pink or purple clusters.
seasonality.summer: Continues blooming through summer with peak flowering in early to mid-summer. Foliage remains attractive with distinctive spotted pattern clearly visible.
seasonality.fall: May produce a second flush of flowers in cooler weather. Leaves may take on reddish tints while maintaining their characteristic silver markings.
seasonality.winter: In mild winters, some leaves may persist, appearing darker and less vibrant but still showing the spotted pattern. Stems die back in harsh cold.

funFact: Despite being called a 'deadnettle,' this plant is actually a fantastic pollinator magnet - its flowers are specifically designed with a landing platform and nectar guides to attract bees, and the long tubular shape makes it a favorite of long-tongued bumblebees who can reach the sweet nectar inside!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with stinging nettle, but spotted deadnettle won't sting you and has the telltale silvery leaf markings that stinging nettle lacks. Memory trick: 'Spotted and soft, stinging nettle is not!'
contextualKnowledge: Originally from Europe and Asia, spotted deadnettle was brought to North America as a garden plant and has naturalized in many areas. While some consider it invasive, it's generally well-behaved in shaded areas and provides valuable early-season nectar for pollinators when few other flowers are available.
compareHints: Among its deadnettle relatives, spotted deadnettle is the only one with distinctive silvery-white leaf markings - red deadnettle and henbit have plain green leaves. White deadnettle is much taller and more upright, while yellow archangel has yellow flowers and different leaf patterns. The spotted leaves make this species unmistakable in the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red deadnettle differs from other Lamium species by its stalked, triangular-heart-shaped leaves and consistent purple-pink flower color.
Among the deadnettles, henbit is unique for its stem-clasping upper leaves - red deadnettle has all stalked leaves, while white and spotted deadnettles are much larger perennial plants.

Yellow archangel stands out from its deadnettle relatives primarily by its golden flowers - red deadnettle has pink-purple blooms, henbit has smaller purple flowers, and white deadnettle has white flowers.
Among the deadnettles, cutleaf deadnettle stands out for its dramatically dissected leaves - much more deeply cut than red deadnettle's heart-shaped leaves or henbit's rounded, scalloped ones.
White deadnettle stands out from its relatives by its pure white flowers and perennial growth habit.
